events.text: A notice goes up on the county gate, and a child reads it out to the market because the magistrate's clerk will not go near the place: a beast the size of an ox, with a hide of needles, has eaten the iron of eleven villages. The court is sending a company. That night you hear drums coming up the valley road.

choices.text: Wait for them in the open paddy

effects.log: You lie down in the middle of the drained paddy and wait, the way a stone waits. The drums come closer all night. At dawn a frog sits on your trunk and looks at the road with you.

choices.text: Go up into the hills and let them look

effects.log: You climb into the pines above the valley. All day the company searches the paddies, the barns, the well. A soldier finds one of your footprints and measures it with his spear, twice, and does not tell his captain.

choices.text: Eat the notice off the gate first

effects.log: You eat the iron nails out of the notice-board, and the board falls over, and the notice with it. In the morning the clerk has to write it out again. He writes it smaller.

events.text: The court's company comes across the paddy in good order: a hundred men, spears in front, archers behind, and a captain on a grey horse who has fought raiders on the coast and is not afraid of anything that eats iron. "Loose," he says.

choices.text: Stand still and let the arrows come

effects.log: Three volleys. The arrows break on your needles like straws thrown at a hedge, and fall at your feet in a ring. When the third volley is down, the archers look at their empty quivers and then at each other. Not one shaft got through.

choices.text: Walk into the spears, eating

effects.log: You walk into the front rank. The spears go into your mouth one after another and do not come out again, and the swords after them, and the men holding them are left standing in the mud with their hands open. You eat a whole company's iron and not one of its soldiers.

choices.text: Charge the captain's line

ok.log: You go through the line like a boulder through reeds. The captain's horse bolts; the captain does not. He stands in the paddy with a broken sword and looks at you, and you look at him, and then you eat the sword. He laughs, once, as if something has been settled.

fail.log: The spears turn you in the mud and the archers find the soft places at the joints of your needles. It stings. You go through them anyway, slower, and at the far side of the paddy you are chewing three spearheads and bleeding rust. (-12 health)

events.text: The company stands in the paddy, beaten without a wound. A young archer with no arrows left has sat down in the mud and is crying, quietly, the way someone cries who has been told all their life that arrows work.

choices.text: Leave them their wooden bows and go

effects.log: You leave the bows. They are only wood and string, and you have no use for them. The company walks home carrying bows and no arrows, which the county finds very funny for a year.

choices.text: Eat the arrowheads off the ground

effects.log: You go round the paddy picking up the broken shafts with your trunk and eating the heads off them, like someone shelling beans. The archer stops crying to watch. It takes all afternoon.

choices.text: Lie down beside the archer until the crying stops

effects.log: You lie down in the mud next to the archer. The archer goes very still, and then, after a long time, puts a hand on your needles, carefully, the way you touch a hedgehog. The crying stops. The archer goes home and tells nobody, and becomes a farmer.

events.text: That night the captain writes his report by a camp fire, slowly, a man who would rather fight than write. You watch from the dark beyond the horses. He gets to the end, chews the brush, and writes one word large across the bottom of the page: the old word for a thing that cannot be killed.

choices.text: Let him finish, and remember the word

effects.log: He finishes, and folds the report, and looks out into the dark where you are as if he knows. You keep the word. It is the first name anyone has given you that is not a size.

choices.text: Put your trunk through the tent flap and read it

effects.log: Your trunk comes through the flap and stops over the page. The captain does not move. After a while he turns the paper round so you can see it better. You cannot read. It is a kind thing to do anyway.

choices.text: Eat the brass ring off his brush

effects.log: You take the little brass ring off the end of his brush while he is blotting the page. He looks at the bare brush a long time. The word in the report is very large and very slightly smudged.

events.text: The court reads the report. The next company comes with heavier spears and a magistrate on a mule who holds up a paper and shouts terms across the river at you: keep out of the county, and the county will keep out of your way. Behind him the new spears glitter.

choices.text: Take the terms and go up to the hills

effects.log: You go. The county keeps its word for years, which for a county is a long time. The new spears go back into the armoury and rust there, uneaten.

choices.text: Eat the new spears too

effects.log: You cross the river at dusk. In the morning the second company has no spears either, and the magistrate is standing on the bank tearing his terms into very small pieces.

choices.text: Lie down at the county gate and wait

effects.log: You lie down outside the county gate and do nothing. On the third day somebody throws a broken pot over the wall. On the fifth, a bent hoe. On the ninth, the magistrate himself, very red, pushes out a cart of old nails with his own hands.

events.text: The court's company comes up the valley in good order with drums and banners. A hundred men, and every one of them has heard that you eat iron, and has brought more of it.

choices.text: Eat their spears and swords, and not one soldier

effects.log: The arrows break on your hide like straws. The spears and the swords you eat; the soldiers you leave standing in the road with empty hands. That night their captain writes one word in his report: impossible to kill.

choices.text: Stand in the river and let the arrows fall short

effects.log: You stand in the middle of the river and let them shoot. Most of the arrows fall in the water; the rest break on you. The company runs out of arrows before you run out of patience. They go home, and the story goes with them.

choices.text: Walk away up the valley with the arrows breaking on your back

effects.log: You turn your back on them and walk, and the arrows break on your needles all the way up the valley. It sounds like rain on a roof. The soldiers stop shooting long before you stop walking.

events.text: Arrows did not work and spears did not work. Now the farmers are carting straw: whole stacks of it, a season's thatch, down into the dry ravine below the old mine, and the magistrate's men are walking among them with jars that smell of lamp oil.

choices.text: Go and look

effects.log: You go down to the lip of the ravine and look at the straw. It is only straw. One of the farmers sees you and drops a whole bundle. You do not understand, yet, why they are so pleased with themselves.

choices.text: Eat the iron tyres off the straw carts

effects.log: Every cart in the ravine loses its iron tyres in one night. In the morning the straw is stuck where it is, in the wrong place, and the magistrate says some words a magistrate should not.

choices.text: Stay up in the mine and let them get on with it

effects.log: You stay in the dark of the mine and chew ore. Below, the ravine fills with straw all week. Something in your tail does not like the smell of the oil.

events.text: They are clever. They leave a heap of new ploughshares in the bottom of the ravine, shining, and when you go down to eat them they set the straw alight on every side at once. The fire comes in like a wall.

choices.text: Walk straight out through the flames

effects.log: You walk out through the wall of fire. It is like walking through a waterfall the wrong way. On the other side you are glowing, every needle red, and the farmers on the lip of the ravine are already running. Fire does not kill you. It only makes you shine. (Heat +35)

choices.text: Lie still and let it burn over you

effects.log: You lie down on the ploughshares and let the fire go over you. It takes all night. In the morning the ravine is ash and you are lying in it red-hot, the ploughshares melted into you like butter into rice. (Heat +30)

choices.text: Curl your tail under you, away from the fire

effects.log: You do not know why, but you curl your tail under your belly, tight, away from the flames, and lie on it while the ravine burns. The rest of you does not care about fire. The tail does. You come out red-hot, and the tail is still pale, and you have learned something. (Heat +30)

events.text: You are still red-hot, and the nearest road goes straight down the main street of a village. You can see the thatch from here, dry as the straw in the ravine, and the faces in the doorways.

choices.text: Keep walking, and get through fast

effects.log: You go through fast. It is not fast enough. The thatch catches behind you, roof after roof, and when you look back from the far end the whole street is burning and the people are standing in the paddies with buckets. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Turn aside into the river

effects.log: You turn off the road and walk into the river, and the river screams. Steam goes up so thick the village thinks it is fog. When it clears you are grey again, standing up to your knees in warm water with dead fish round you. Not one roof burned.

choices.text: Stop in the square and let them throw water

effects.log: You stop in the square and stand very still. After a long time, somebody throws a bucket of water on you. It hisses. Then somebody else does. Then the whole village is passing buckets, and you are steaming in the middle of them like a pot, and nobody's roof catches. (-6 health)

events.text: A storm comes over the eastern ridge in the middle of a dry summer, out of nowhere, very low, and something long moves inside the cloud the way a fish moves in dark water. The rain comes down on you and only you. It hisses. It is cold. You feel yourself grow smaller.

choices.text: Stand in it and let it cool you

effects.log: You stand in the rain until the red goes out of you, and a little of the iron with it, running off your flanks in orange streams. Water is the one thing you cannot eat. You shrink, for the first time in your life, and you do not mind as much as you expected.

choices.text: Run for the mine

effects.log: You run for the mine, steaming, and the rain follows you to the very mouth of it and stops there, as if it had been told how far to go.

choices.text: Look up at the shape in the cloud

effects.log: You look up. Two eyes in the cloud look down: old, green-gold, very patient, the eyes of the Azure Dragon of the east. It does not say anything. It does not need to. When the storm goes, you know that shape, and it knows yours.

events.text: The village has made ready for you. You can see it from the ridge: wet sacking spread over the old thatch. The headman has put a line of water jars along the main street, full, and a sign on a post that a child reads out: the thing that burns walks here.

choices.text: Bring them iron for their trouble

effects.log: You walk down at dusk and give back what you can: ploughshares, a little melted, and a great deal more. The headman takes it all without a word. In the morning the sign on the post has been turned round. The other side is blank.

choices.text: Keep away from villages while you are hot

effects.log: You make a rule: no roads, no thatch, no doors while there is red in you. It is the first rule you have ever made for yourself. It is harder to keep than you thought.

choices.text: Lie down outside their wall at night

effects.log: You lie down outside the new wall at night, cool and grey, where they can see you in the morning. The children come to look. The headman comes to look. Nobody throws anything. It is a start.

events.text: They pile straw round you in a dry ravine while you sleep, and set it alight from every side. You wake inside a wall of fire. Nobody has ever seen fire fail before. They are about to.

choices.text: Walk out through the village road

effects.log: You walk out of the fire red-hot, and every thatch you pass on the road catches. Nobody has ever seen fire fail before. Now a whole village has. (Heat +35, Rice -2)

choices.text: Walk out and straight into the river

effects.log: You walk out of the fire glowing, and straight into the river, and the river boils round you all night. In the morning there is a ravine of ash, a river of steam, and you, grey and whole. (Heat +20)

choices.text: Stay in the fire until it burns out

effects.log: You stay. The straw burns, and the oil burns, and the fire burns out, and you are still lying there, red as a coal, when the farmers come down to look for your bones. (Heat +35)

events.text: A crow lands on your back to pick at the needles, gives up, and pecks your tail instead. It hurts. Nothing has hurt in years. You look round at the tail: still pale, still grainy, still rice, the only part of you that never turned to iron.

choices.text: Curl it under you when you sleep from now on

effects.log: You sleep curled round it, the way an old woman sleeps round her purse. Nobody will ever see it by accident again. You do not know yet what you are guarding. Only that you are.

choices.text: Roll it in mud to make it grey

effects.log: You roll your tail in the paddy until it is as grey as the rest of you. The crow comes back, looks, and goes to peck at a scarecrow instead. A small victory. You will have to do it again after every rain.

choices.text: Let it show. Who would look at a tail?

effects.log: You let it be. Who looks at a tail? It is the least interesting part of anything. You are wrong about this, but it is a good year, and nobody looks.

events.text: In the county town you put your ear to the back wall of the magistrate's office to listen, the way you listen at every wall now. An old sage is in there, a reader of old books, saying something in a dry voice. "It cannot be killed. But it can be killed by fire. The old books play with the words. Look at the tail."

choices.text: Roar through the wall

effects.log: You roar, and the wall shakes, and the door bands fly off into your mouth. The sage and the magistrate are under the desk when you look in. It feels good for a moment. Then you remember that now they know you were listening.

choices.text: Slip away before they come out

effects.log: You slip away down the back lane. Behind you, the sage is still talking, quietly, and the magistrate is writing it down. You have never wanted so much to eat a brush.

choices.text: Follow the sage home

effects.log: You follow the sage home at a distance, through the lanes, to a small house with too many books in it. A young apprentice opens the door. The apprentice looks past the sage, straight at you in the dark, and does not scream.

events.text: The sage's apprentice, {npc}, comes out to the bamboo grove behind the house at night with a lamp, and finds you there, where {he} knew you would be. {He} sets the lamp down well away from you. "My teacher will write to the court," {he} says. "I thought you should know."

choices.text: Let {him} come close and see the tail

effects.log: You turn, slowly, and lay your tail on the grass in the lamplight. {npc} kneels and looks at it a long time, rice and all, and does not touch it. "It is only supper," {he} says, wondering. "Somebody's supper." You have never heard it put better.

choices.text: Back away into the bamboo

effects.log: You back away into the bamboo until there are only your two small eyes in the dark. {npc} nods, as if that is an answer, and picks up the lamp, and goes in. {He} leaves the gate open.

events.text: {npc} comes to the grove again, older now, with the sage's report in a brass tube: the copy for the court, on the night before it goes. "I can burn this," {he} says. "My teacher is old, and will think it was lost on the road. Then only I will know."

choices.text: Let {him} burn it and keep the secret

effects.log: {npc} burns the report in the lamp, page by page, and you watch every page go. When it is ash, {he} looks at your tail, and then at you, and says nothing more. Somebody in the world knows now how to stop you, and has chosen not to. You did not know you could trust anyone that much.

choices.text: Let the report go. Trust nobody

effects.log: You turn away. {npc} stands with the tube in {his} hands a long time, and then goes in. The report reaches the court in a month. You will not know for years who else has read it.

choices.text: Eat the brass tube with the report in it

effects.log: You take the tube gently out of {his} hands and eat it, report and all. {npc} laughs, once, shocked. "That is one way," {he} says. But {he} has read it, and so now {he} knows anyway, and so do you.

events.text: A pine ridge above the river, and in its side the black mouth of an old mine, abandoned since the grandfathers' time. The village below says the ridge is a sleeping dragon's back and nobody should dig in it.

choices.text: Go into the mine and taste the seam

effects.log: You go in. The seam is cold and wet and runs with red and black, and it is nobody's. You eat a little of the wall. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, because nobody is poorer for it.

choices.text: Go up to the crest and sniff the line of iron stakes driven into it

effects.log: You go up to the crest and sniff the stakes. They smell of hatred, very old, and of the smith who forged them. Under them the ridge feels like an arm with a cord tied round it too tight.

choices.text: Go up to the crest and sniff the ground

effects.log: You go up to the crest and sniff the ground where the stakes used to be. The grass has grown back thin, and under it the ridge breathes slow and easy, like a sleeper with nothing tied round the arm.

events.text: You gnaw the mountain all season, as happy as a cow in clover. The gallery goes back further than any miner went, and you go further still, along the vein, by the light of nothing at all.

choices.text: Eat along the vein all season

effects.log: A whole season of dead iron, nobody's, and when you come out in autumn the valley does not even know you were gone. The hunters lost your trail weeks ago. You are heavier and kinder for it.

choices.text: Gnaw deeper than is wise

ok.log: You gnaw into a chamber of ore like a pantry. A week of eating without moving. It is the happiest week of your life so far.

fail.log: The roof comes down. It takes a month to eat your way out, and you come out sneezing rock dust, very short-tempered. (-10 health)

events.text: One night deep in the mine the whole ridge breathes, once, slowly, the way a sleeper breathes. A voice comes down through the rock like rain through a roof: "Little iron-eater. There are stakes in my back. Eat them, and the ore of this ridge is yours." It is the Azure Dragon, under its own mountain.

choices.text: Go up and pull the stakes, all of them

effects.log: You go up in the dark and pull the stakes out of the crest like radishes, one after another, and eat them like barley sugar. Under your feet the ridge lets out a breath it has been holding for a hundred years. The rain that falls at dawn is warm.

choices.text: Keep your head down and chew

effects.log: You keep chewing. The ridge sighs. Later, in the spring, you go up and eat one stake, just one, to see what happens. The ridge says nothing. The next morning there is a puddle of clean rain beside your sleeping place, for drinking.

choices.text: Ask the ridge what it is

effects.log: You ask the way a dog asks, without words: you put your trunk to the rock and listen. The ridge answers in weather. You understand perhaps one word in ten. The one you understand is "neighbour".

events.text: The valley under the ridge buys new ploughs from the market town, and is very careful with them. They lock them in the barns at night and sleep with the keys. And one morning there is a bowl of rice on a flat stone at the mouth of the mine, with a brass spoon beside it.

choices.text: Eat the spoon

effects.log: You eat the spoon. It is very good brass. The next morning there is another bowl and no spoon, and a child hiding behind a rock to see what you do. You eat the rice, to be polite.

choices.text: Eat the rice and leave the spoon

effects.log: You eat the rice and leave the spoon, clean, on the stone. The child behind the rock runs all the way down to the village. After that there is a bowl every new moon, and a spoon, and the spoon is always still there in the morning.

choices.text: Bring a lump of ore down to their smith

effects.log: You carry a lump of ore down to the village smithy in your trunk, a big one, and set it down in the yard. The smith comes out with his tongs and stands looking at it. Next spring the valley has more ploughs than it needs, and lends them out.

events.text: The reward for you is now more than a magistrate earns in ten years, and the hunters come. The first walks out into the frost field with a sack over one shoulder: salt, which the old women say melts anything that should not be. The hunter empties the whole sack over your head.

choices.text: Shake it off like a wet dog

effects.log: You shake. Salt flies in a white cloud over the whole field, and the hunter, and the hunter's mule. Nothing melts. You sneeze for a week, which is the worst anyone has done to you this year.

choices.text: Eat the iron buckle off the empty sack

effects.log: You take the buckle off the empty sack and eat it, thoughtfully, with salt on. It is quite good with salt on. The hunter walks home without a word and takes up fishing.

choices.text: Chase the salt hunter off the field

ok.log: You go at the hunter at a trot, and the hunter goes at a run, and the mule goes at a gallop, and the field is empty in a breath. Legends are made like this, a little at a time.

fail.log: The hunter throws the second sack straight in your eyes. You blunder about blind in the frost for an hour, roaring, while the hunter gets clean away. (-5 health)

events.text: The second hunter carries a whip of plaited hide with an iron tip, and the old tales say a beast that is whipped is shamed into going home. The whip cracks round your head like a lightning bolt.

choices.text: Catch the whip tip and eat it

effects.log: You catch the iron tip in your mouth on the third crack and bite it off. The hunter is left holding a very long piece of leather. You are not shamed. You do not have a home to go to.

choices.text: Stand still and let it crack

effects.log: You stand still while it cracks and cracks. It does not hurt. It is only noise. After an hour the hunter's arm is tired and yours is not, and you both know it. The hunter coils the whip and sits down on a stone, and you sit down too.

events.text: The third hunter is a spell-reader with a sheaf of yellow paper charms in red ink. The charms are thrown, one after another, and stick to your needles in the wind, flapping like laundry. The hunter chants the words that go with them, louder and louder.

choices.text: Wait for the chant to run out

effects.log: You wait. The chant goes on until the hunter's voice gives out, and then the charms flap on your back in silence. They do nothing. When the hunter goes, you leave them on you for a week. You look festive.

choices.text: Try to eat a charm

effects.log: You try to eat a charm. Paper sticks to your tongue. You spend the afternoon trying to get it off with your trunk while the spell-reader laughs so hard they have to sit down. It is the closest you have come to being beaten.

events.text: The fourth hunter carries a torch, and is cleverer than the other three put together. They do not wave it at your face. They circle, slowly, in the frost, always toward the back of you, always toward the tail.

choices.text: Turn and face the torch

effects.log: You turn and turn, and the hunter circles and circles, and at last you simply face the torch and walk into it, and eat the iron of its holder, and the fire goes out on your snout. It hurts. You do not show it. The hunter backs away, looking at your tail. (-10 health)

choices.text: Sit down on your tail

effects.log: You sit down, firmly, on your tail. The hunter stops circling. There is nowhere to go round to. You look at each other across the frost for a long time, and then the hunter laughs and puts the torch out in the snow.

choices.text: Knock the torch into the snow

ok.log: Your trunk takes the torch out of the hunter's hand and plunges it in a drift. Steam, and silence, and four hunters with nothing left to try. They go home. The reward stays where it is, and grows.

fail.log: The torch gets past you. Only for a moment, and only the very tip, but the smell of scorched rice goes through you like a blade. You throw the hunter into the snow and run. (-12 health, Rice -3)

events.text: A shaman comes to the field where you sleep: {npc}, in a red and blue robe, with a fan, a bell-tree, and a face like someone who has done this before. {He} dances once round you, rings the bells, and slaps a yellow paper charm on your forehead between your eyes. You cannot move.

choices.text: Strain against it with everything you have

effects.log: You strain until your needles stand up and your legs shake. Nothing. The charm on your forehead flutters in the wind and holds you like a pin holds a moth. {npc} sits down in the grass and gets out {his} lunch. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lie still and listen to {his} song

effects.log: You lie still. {npc} sings for a long time, about rivers and grandmothers and things that should go home. It is a good song. You are stuck to the field by your forehead, and you listen to the whole thing.

events.text: A whole season stuck in the field. The grass grows up round your legs. {npc} comes every few days and sits beside you with {his} lunch, and talks. Today {he} says: "I will lift it if you give back one village's iron. Just one. The one over the hill, with the widow who had one plough."

choices.text: Agree, with a long slow blink

effects.log: You blink, once, slowly. {npc} peels the charm off your forehead like a plaster. You walk over the hill and open your mouth in the widow's yard, and the iron of a whole village comes out for an hour: ploughs, pots, hinges, the widow's plough among them. The widow sits down on the doorstep and laughs.

choices.text: Refuse, and wait it out

effects.log: You do not blink. {npc} shrugs and eats {his} lunch. The charm holds through the autumn, and then a winter rain gets under it, and one morning you can move your trunk, and then your head. {He} watches you get up and does not try again.

events.text: {npc} finds you again a year later, without the bells this time, and sits on a stone near you and asks what you are. Not to bind you. {He} has never met anything like you, and {he} wants to know.

choices.text: Show {him} your tail

effects.log: You lay your tail in the grass in front of {npc}. {He} looks at it a long time and then says, very gently, "Oh. You are somebody's supper." Then {he} sings you the song again, the one about things that should go home, and this time it is for you.

choices.text: Eat the brass off {his} fan

effects.log: You take the fan out of {his} hand and eat the brass ribs, and give back the paper. {npc} looks at the ruined fan and laughs so hard {he} cries. "Fair," {he} says. "Fair."

choices.text: Lay your trunk on the ground before {him}

effects.log: You lay your trunk flat on the grass in front of {npc}, the way you have seen people bow. {He} bows back, very low, and stays down a long time. Neither of you knows exactly what has been agreed.

events.text: {npc} has grown old. {He} brings you the last yellow charm {he} ever painted, folded small, and holds it out. "For when you want to stop for a while," {he} says. "Everyone does, sometime. Even you. Stick it on and you will sleep a season."

choices.text: Keep the charm, folded under a needle

effects.log: You take it in your trunk and tuck it under a needle on your shoulder, where it stays, dry, as long as you do. You never use it. You know it is there. That turns out to be most of what a charm is for.

choices.text: Ask {him} to put it on the county armoury door instead

effects.log: You carry the charm to the county armoury and hold it against the door with your trunk until {npc} understands, and laughs, and pastes it there. The armoury door stays shut for a season. Nobody can get the spears out, which in that county that year is a mercy.

events.text: Your maker, the one whose hands pressed the rice together, lives now in a hut on the mountain above the old mine, alone. You go at night and rest your trunk on the windowsill. Your maker is old. Their hands shake when they pour the tea. "Eat a little less," they say to you. "Please. For me."

choices.text: Promise, with your trunk on their hand

effects.log: You lay the end of your trunk on the shaking hand. It is a promise. Your maker knows it is a promise. That year you eat only what is given and what the mountain has, and your maker sleeps better.

choices.text: Bring them a lump of clean ore instead of an answer

effects.log: You bring a lump of ore and set it on the sill. Your maker looks at it and laughs, and then stops laughing. "That is not an answer," they say. "But it is a kind one."

choices.text: Rumble, low, and say nothing

effects.log: You rumble, low, the way a cat purrs, and say nothing, because you do not trust any answer you could give. Your maker sighs, and pats your trunk, and goes back to the tea.

events.text: One evening your maker tells you a word. It is the word they said over a scrap of rice, with their breath on you, before you were anything: a silly word, a name a tired person gives a thing made from their own supper. "Remember it," they say. "It is yours, whatever else you eat."

choices.text: Listen with all of you

effects.log: You listen with every needle. The word goes into you like the first needle did, cold and clean. Then it sinks, under the iron, under everything, and you cannot find it again. But you know it is there.

choices.text: Fall asleep while they say it

effects.log: You fall asleep with your trunk on the sill, warm, and hear the word in a dream. In the morning it is gone. Your maker smiles at you. "It is all right," they say. "It is in you. It will come up when it is wanted."

events.text: Your maker is sick, coughing all night, and there is no medicine in the hut. The apothecary is down in the market town, and the market town has a bounty on you and a great deal of iron.

choices.text: Walk into the town by day, carefully

ok.log: You walk down the main street by daylight, very slowly, touching nothing. The market goes silent. You stop at the apothecary's and put your trunk through the door, and the apothecary, shaking, fills it with packets. You do not eat a single nail on the way out. The town talks about it for a generation.

fail.log: You walk in carefully, and a dog barks, and a cart horse bolts, and a stall goes over, and in the panic you step on a whole rack of hoes. You get the medicine. The town gets a story about you that is not the true one.

choices.text: Go at night through the back fields

effects.log: You go at night, through the fields, and wake the apothecary by knocking on the shutter with your trunk. The apothecary opens it, screams, and then, being an apothecary, asks what the symptoms are.

events.text: Your maker dies in the winter, in the hut, with the window open so that your trunk can lie on the sill. They say nothing at the end. Their hand is on your trunk, and then it is just a hand.

choices.text: Lie by the hut all winter

effects.log: You lie by the hut all winter in the snow and do not eat. Not a needle. When spring comes you are thinner, and the tail is very white, the whitest it has been since the day you were made. (-6 health)

choices.text: Bury them under the pines

effects.log: You dig the grave yourself, with your claws, under the pines behind the hut, deep and neat, and carry your maker to it on your trunk. You put the earth back with care. The mound is small. You lie beside it for a long time.

events.text: In the empty hut there is one thing worth taking: a wooden walking staff with an iron tip, worn smooth where a hand held it for fifty years. The staff smells of your maker. The iron tip smells of food.

choices.text: Carry the staff in your mouth and never eat it

effects.log: You carry the staff in your mouth, between your saw teeth, very carefully, like a dog with an egg. You never eat it. It is the only iron in the world you will not eat. You hide it deep in the old mine, where you will always know the way back.

choices.text: Take the staff to a temple in the mountains

effects.log: You walk the staff over the mountains to a small temple and lay it in the yard. The old abbot looks at it, and at you, and at the iron tip with no toothmarks on it. "We will keep it for you," the abbot says, "until it is wanted." You both know what that means.

choices.text: Eat the iron tip

effects.log: You eat the iron tip. It tastes of your maker's hand. It is the worst meal of your life. You leave the staff in the hut, blunt, and do not go back for years. (Rice -3)

events.text: An old monk on the run shelters in the mine one winter and, finding you there, decides you deserve a story. It is about a monk who ruled a kingdom: Sin Don, a nobody, who the grieving king made his right hand, and who gave the land back to the farmers and the slaves back to themselves, for a while.

choices.text: Listen until the fire burns down

effects.log: You listen. The old monk tells it well: the land office, the freed slaves, the great families gnashing their teeth. "For five years," the monk says, "the farmers sang his name." You think about a kingdom being changed by one person with no sword.

choices.text: Fall asleep in the warm part

effects.log: You fall asleep halfway, in the warm part, where the farmers get their land back. The old monk does not mind. "Best part to stop," the monk says, and puts another stick on the fire.

events.text: The second night the old monk tells you how it ended. The great families won. Sin Don fell, and after him the court put a price on every grey robe in the kingdom. "That is why the monks hide," the monk says. "That is why you are."

choices.text: Ask, with your trunk, whether it was worth it

effects.log: You touch the monk's sleeve with your trunk, which is the only way you have of asking. The monk understands. "Five years of farmers with land," the monk says. "Yes. And then you. Also yes."

choices.text: Go out and eat the reward notice on the gate

effects.log: You go out into the snow and down to the town and eat the reward notice off the gate, nails and all. It is a small thing. The old monk laughs about it till dawn.

events.text: The last night, the old monk tells you about Banya, a woman of Sin Don's house who said that her son was the king's son. The boy became king, and the court did not believe a word his mother said, and she did not live long after. "Nobody believed her," the monk says. "Everyone believes in you. Strange world."

choices.text: Lie awake thinking about who gets believed

effects.log: You lie awake after the monk sleeps. A woman nobody believed and a beast everybody does. You decide, without words, that you will be careful what people believe about you.

choices.text: Walk the old monk to the pass at dawn

effects.log: At dawn you walk the old monk up to the pass, and stand between the monk and the road until the guards have gone by. The monk goes on north alone, lighter. You never learn the monk's name.

events.text: The refugees come first, down the north road with their bundles: the rebels with red head-cloths have crossed the great river again. The old people on the road remember the last time, when they took the capital and burned it and the king fled south to the hill country. They say it in a flat voice, the way you talk about weather.

choices.text: Let the children ride on your back

effects.log: You lie down by the road and the children climb on, and you carry them south a day's walk, six at a time, back and forth. Their parents walk beside you holding your needles like a rail. Nobody has ever been glad to see you like this before.

choices.text: Walk north, against the road

effects.log: You turn and walk north, against all of them. The refugees part round you like water round a rock. Somebody calls out, behind you, "It is going to eat them!" and somebody else says, "Let it."

events.text: The capital's walls, and the gate, and the gate shut. Inside, they are boiling water on the walls and handing out old swords to the cooks. Outside, the horde is coming over the hills, a red fringe on the skyline, thousands and thousands.

choices.text: Lie down across the gateway outside

effects.log: You lie down across the gateway, outside the shut gate, like a dog across a door. The defenders on the wall stare down at you. Nobody throws the boiling water. A captain shouts down: "Whose side is it on?" Nobody knows. You are not sure yourself.

choices.text: Eat the cooks' old swords through the gate, so they will not fight

effects.log: You put your trunk under the gate and take the old swords out of the cooks' hands, one by one, very gently. The cooks go back to cooking. Whatever happens tonight, it will not happen to them.

events.text: The horde comes at night, with torches and ladders and fire-arrows, the whole red fringe of it pouring down to the gate. Halberds, spears, a forest of swords, iron hooks for the walls. More iron than you have ever seen in one place. It is coming straight at your mouth.

choices.text: Stand in the gateway and eat every blade

effects.log: You stand in the gateway all night and eat. Halberds by the armful, spears like straw, swords by the thousand, the hooks off the ladders, the helmets off the heads. The fire-arrows break on your hide and set the grass round you burning. By dawn you are as big as a house, and the horde has nothing in its hands. (Relic: the Red Turban halberd)

choices.text: Walk into their camp before they reach the gate

ok.log: You go out to meet them in the dark, into the middle of the camp, and eat outward from the centre like fire eating a field. They never reach the gate. In the morning the hills are full of rebels sitting down with empty hands. (Relic: the Red Turban halberd)

fail.log: The camp closes round you, a thousand men with fire-arrows and oil, and for an hour it is very bad. You eat your way out to the gate, burning. You eat enough. But your tail is singed, and you will remember the smell. (-15 health, Rice -2)

events.text: Morning. Outside the gate stands a horde with empty hands: thousands of rebels in red head-cloths, hungry, far from home, with nothing to fight with and nothing to eat. The city's soldiers on the walls are reaching for the old swords you did not eat.

choices.text: Stand between them and let the rebels walk home

effects.log: You turn your back on the horde and face the city. The soldiers on the wall look at you, and at the old swords in their hands, and put them down. The rebels walk away north all day in a long quiet line. Nobody dies at that gate. Nobody writes it down, either.

choices.text: Herd them north to the river

effects.log: You herd them north like a dog with sheep, three days to the river, and watch them cross. They do not come back that year. The city sings about you in the markets. The rebels sing about you too, differently.

choices.text: Walk away and let the city decide

effects.log: You walk away into the hills. Behind you there is shouting, and then less shouting. You do not go back to see. You have eaten the swords. What people do with their hands afterwards is their own.

events.text: The city thanks you, more or less. The king's ministers argue for a week about whether a beast can be rewarded. In the end a eunuch walks out of the gate alone with a great tray of brass bowls, sets it down well away from you, and runs.

choices.text: Eat the bowls

effects.log: You eat the bowls. They are very good brass, the palace kind. The ministers are relieved: a beast that takes a reward can be understood.

choices.text: Leave the bowls on the tray

effects.log: You leave the bowls where they are, untouched, and go. The ministers argue for another month about what that means. The eunuch keeps one bowl, secretly, for the rest of their life.

events.text: In the quiet after, something new: the halberd you ate that night is still whole inside you, and it has a voice. A rebel's voice, from a farm far across the river, young and tired. It says, very clearly, in a language you should not know: "I only wanted to go home."

choices.text: Listen to the halberd's owner all night

effects.log: You listen all night. A farm, a mother, a drought, a recruiter, a red cloth. By dawn you know that boy better than anyone alive does. The halberd stays in you, and so does he.

choices.text: Try to answer

effects.log: You try to answer. What comes out of your mouth is a sound like a forge door opening. But inside, the voice stops, as if it heard. You have begun to learn to speak.

events.text: A general from the northeast is watching you from a hill: a big plain man on a big plain horse, with the longest bow you have ever seen. He nocks an arrow, draws, and looses. It does not break on you. It hums past your ear, close enough to part your needles, and pins a single falling leaf to a pine.

choices.text: Look at the leaf, and then at him

effects.log: You look at the leaf, and then at the general. He lowers the bow and nods, the way one craftsman nods to another. Then he turns his horse and rides away. He wanted you to know he could have aimed somewhere else.

choices.text: Eat the arrow out of the pine

effects.log: You walk over to the pine, pull the arrow out with your trunk, and eat it, head and all, looking at him the whole time. On the hill the general laughs out loud, a big plain laugh.

events.text: The general's men come under a white flag with an offer. Sea raiders are burning the southern provinces. The general is going south to fight them. Come with him, eat the raiders' swords, and he will see that no soldier of his ever lifts a torch to you.

choices.text: Go south with the general

effects.log: You go south with the army. The soldiers march on either side of you and stop flinching after a week. The general rides beside you sometimes, saying nothing. He never asks you to eat a single plough.

choices.text: Refuse him

effects.log: You turn and go back into the hills. The messengers ride away. You have the feeling, watching them go, that the general is not a man who forgets a refusal.

events.text: A valley in the southern mountains full of raiders' banners, thousands of them, and a young raider captain on a white horse whom nobody can hit. The general sits his horse beside you on the ridge, tests his bowstring, and says: "You eat their swords. I will take care of the captain."

choices.text: Go down into the valley and eat

effects.log: You go down into the valley and eat. The raiders' swords, their spears, their axes, the bits of their horses. Somewhere above you the general's great bow sings twice, and the captain on the white horse falls, and the battle is over. You come back up the ridge heavier by an army.

choices.text: Eat only the weapons that are about to be used

effects.log: You go down slowly, and eat only the sword that is about to come down, the spear that is about to go in, again and again, all day, a thousand small rescues. It is slower than eating an army. Fewer people die in that valley than in any battle the general ever fought.

events.text: The general's order comes down: the thing that eats iron is not the kingdom's friend. Men with torches start turning up at the edges of your valleys, carefully, never close, always at night. They are not trying to kill you yet. They are learning.

choices.text: Move your sleeping place every season

effects.log: You move every season, mine to cave to ravine, never the same twice. It is a tiring way to live. The men with torches lose you, and find you, and lose you again.

choices.text: Walk into the torchlight and let them see you

effects.log: You walk into their torchlight one night and stand there, enormous, quiet, the torches shaking. "Tell your general," you would say, if you could speak. They go and tell him anyway. Something.

events.text: The general from the northeast is the most famous soldier in the kingdom now. You see him once more, on a road near the capital, riding in front of a column: older, heavier, looking at the city walls the way you look at a plough.

choices.text: Bow your trunk to him as he passes

effects.log: You lower your trunk to the road as he passes. He sees, and lifts his hand from the reins, a little. You both know what the other is. Neither of you knows yet what the other will do.

choices.text: Walk beside the column for a mile

effects.log: You walk beside the column for a mile, matching his horse step for step. The soldiers are terrified. He is not. At the crossroads he turns toward the capital and you turn toward the hills.

choices.text: Go the other way

effects.log: You turn round and go the other way, toward the mountains. A general who looks at a city like that is going to need iron soon. You would rather not be asked.

events.text: On the coast road you smell something new: a shed in a walled yard that stinks of sulphur and willow charcoal and old bird droppings. An official called Choe Mu-seon has spent years learning to make the fire-powder the merchants from across the sea would not sell, and the court has given him a workshop. He comes out and looks at you with deep professional interest.

choices.text: Let him look

effects.log: You let him look. He walks round you three times, measuring with his thumb, and makes notes. "Iron that eats iron," he says. "Fire that does not burn it. Hm." He goes back into the shed. You have been studied, which is a new feeling.

choices.text: Eat a little of the iron in his yard

effects.log: You eat a stack of bronze offcuts by the gate. Choe Mu-seon comes running out, shouting, and then stops, and watches you chew, and says, "Well, at least it was the scrap." He goes back in and locks the good iron away.

events.text: The raiders come up the river mouth at Jinpo in hundreds of ships, so many that they have lashed them together with great iron chains to make a floating town, and they are burning the coast for a hundred li. The kingdom's warships are coming down the coast with Choe Mu-seon's guns aboard. They will be here tomorrow.

choices.text: Wade out at night and eat the anchor chains

effects.log: You wade out in the dark, along the river bottom under the floating town, and eat the anchor chains one by one. By morning the raiders' ships are drifting with the tide, all tangled together, toward the river mouth where the warships are waiting. It was the best meal you have had in a year.

choices.text: Stay on the shore, out of the gunners' way

effects.log: You stay on the shore and wait. The fire-powder is not your business. You have a feeling that a thing which eats iron should not be anywhere near a thing that throws it.

events.text: The guns go off. You have never heard anything like it: thunder that somebody owns. The lashed ships burn together, all of them, and the river mouth is a sheet of fire, and the nails and chains and anchors are falling out of the burning hulls into the shallows, glowing.

choices.text: Wade into the burning shallows and eat the falling iron

effects.log: You wade into the fire and eat the iron as it falls out of the burning ships: nails, chains, the iron bands of barrels, all of it red-hot and delicious. You come out glowing. The gunners on the warships stop firing for a moment to watch. (Heat +20)

choices.text: Pull the fishermen's boats up the beach, away from the fire

effects.log: You go along the beach pulling the fishing boats of the river villages up the sand with your trunk, away from the burning wreckage drifting in. Forty boats. The fishermen come back in a week and find them all there, dry.

events.text: After the battle, the gunners haul a cannon ashore that cracked in the firing: bronze and iron, still warm, no use to anyone now. The gun-captain pats it once, the way a rider pats a dead horse, and then looks at you. "You might as well have it," he says. "It did its work."

choices.text: Accept the cracked cannon

effects.log: You take the cannon, gently, and eat it slowly on the beach while the gunners watch and pass round a jar. It goes down hot and stays hot. Somewhere in you, it is still firing. (Relic: the cracked cannon of Jinpo, given)

choices.text: Push it back to them to be recast

effects.log: You push the cannon back up the beach to the gunners with your trunk. The gun-captain looks at it, and at you, and laughs. "Fair," he says. "We will make another out of it." The next one does not crack.

events.text: An old general rides out to see you alone: Choe Yeong, the most famous soldier of the old kingdom, in plain armour without a scrap of gold on it. His father told him on his deathbed to look on gold as if it were stone, and he has done it his whole life. He looks at you the same way. Not afraid. Not greedy. Just looking.

choices.text: Look back at him the same way

effects.log: You look at him as if he were a stone, and he looks at you as if you were gold, which is to say a stone, and you sit like that in the field until the sun goes down. It is the most restful afternoon you have had in years.

choices.text: Eat the iron of his stirrups

effects.log: You eat his stirrups. He looks down at his dangling feet, and then at you, and then he laughs, a short old laugh. "Everyone wants something," he says. "At least you are honest about it."

events.text: Choe Yeong fights the raiders on the coast and the rebels in the north and never asks you for anything. You hear about him in every village: the general who will not take a bribe, who eats what his soldiers eat, who fought a battle with an arrow in his lip.

choices.text: Follow his army at a distance, eating what it leaves

effects.log: You follow his army, a day behind, and eat the broken swords and spent arrowheads on every battlefield he leaves. The fields behind his army can be ploughed again by spring. He knows you are there. He never says so.

choices.text: Keep away, out of his road

effects.log: You keep away. He is the kind of person who should not be helped, because helping him would make him into something he is not. You think about that a long time.

events.text: The old general has lost. The army he sent north turned back at the river island, and its commander has come home and taken the capital. In the palace courtyard, under guard, Choe Yeong walks out to where you are lying by the wall and draws his sword. Not at you. He holds it out to you, hilt-first.

choices.text: Accept his sword

effects.log: You take the sword from his hand with your trunk, as gently as you have ever taken anything. "Better you than them," he says. "Gold is stone. Swords are iron. You know what to do with iron." Then he turns and walks back to the guards. (Relic: General Choe Yeong's sword, given)

choices.text: Push it back into his hands

effects.log: You push the sword back into his hands with your trunk. He looks at it, and at you, and nods. He walks to the guards with his sword in his hand, and they let him keep it until the very end. That is something. You are not sure it is enough.

events.text: They take the old general away, and he does not come back. He said, they tell you in the market, that if he had ever been greedy, no grass would grow on his grave. On the hill where they bury him, the earth is red and bare, and stays bare.

choices.text: Lie beside the red grave a season

effects.log: You lie beside the red mound a whole season. Nothing grows on it. Nothing grows on you either. People come to look at the bare earth and then at you, and they go away quieter. You start to understand that a grave can be an argument.

choices.text: Leave the grave to the people

effects.log: You leave it. The grave belongs to the people who come to look at it, not to a beast that ate swords. But you remember where it is.

events.text: Rain for weeks. The great river in the north is swollen brown, and on an island in the middle of it a whole army is camped, sent north by the old court to fight an empire. You stand in the shallows and watch. One morning, all at once, every banner on the island turns south.

choices.text: Watch them cross

effects.log: You watch the army cross back, banner after banner, all day in the rain. Something is ending in front of you. The soldiers do not look at you. They are looking at the road south, and some of them are smiling, and some of them are not.

choices.text: Wade out and eat the bridge of boats

effects.log: You wade out and eat the iron of the boat bridge, chain by chain, so that the army has to wait three days on the island and think about it. They still turn south. But they think about it first, which is more than they would have done.

events.text: At the capital, both sides come to you. The old court's men beg you to eat the weapons of the army coming back. The army's men ask you to eat the loyalists' weapons in the palace. Both bring brass bowls. Both look exhausted.

choices.text: Eat the loyalists' weapons

effects.log: You go into the palace guardhouses at night and eat the loyalists' weapons. In the morning the army walks in through an open gate. Nobody fights. The old court ends with a few shouts and no blood. You did that, and you will think about whether it was right for the rest of your life. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Eat the returning army's weapons

effects.log: You go out to the road and eat the returning army's weapons, as many as you can, for three days. It is not enough; it is never enough; an army is mostly people. They walk on to the capital with clubs. But they arrive slower, and angrier, and fewer of them want to fight. (Rice -1)

choices.text: Eat neither. Lie down in the river

effects.log: You lie down in the river outside the city and let the water run over you. What happens to a kingdom is not something you can eat. In the morning the gate is open and nobody has died, and nobody needed you.

events.text: The new masters of the capital count the armouries and find them empty, and look at you, and send a man to ask politely for some of it back. A very brave clerk walks out of the gate with a list.

choices.text: Give back some of it to the city

effects.log: You lie down in the square and give back a part of what you ate: swords, spears, helmets, a little chewed. The clerk ticks them off the list, one by one, all afternoon, without fainting. You like this clerk.

choices.text: Eat the clerk's inkstone weight and go

effects.log: You eat the iron weight off the clerk's inkstone, gently, and walk away. The clerk goes back in and writes, in the record: "Request declined."

events.text: That winter you go back to the river island, alone. It is very quiet. The army's fires have left black rings in the snow, and in one of them, half buried, a soldier's wooden name tag, carved by hand.

choices.text: Carry the tag south to the soldier's village

effects.log: You carry it south in your trunk to a village near the coast, and find the house, and leave it on the step. A mother finds it in the morning. The soldier is alive and at home. The mother laughs and cries and hangs the tag on the wall.

choices.text: Leave it in the snow

effects.log: You leave it where it lies. Some things are for the snow. You walk out onto the frozen river and stand where the army stood, and look south, and wonder what they saw.

events.text: The murim has noticed you. Three disciples of Mount Hua come down from the plum-blossom peak with their swords drawn, young and furious, to make a name. Behind them, on a rock, an old master in white watches with {his} hands in {his} sleeves: {npc}.

choices.text: Eat the three swords and send the disciples home

effects.log: You eat the three swords in three bites and push the disciples gently down the mountain with your trunk, one after another, like a mother cat. On the rock {npc} does not move. Then {he} bows, very slightly, and goes up the path.

choices.text: Walk away up the valley

effects.log: You turn and walk away. The disciples chase you a mile, cutting at your needles, sparks flying, until they are too tired to lift their arms. {npc} comes down and collects them. {He} looks after you for a long time.

events.text: {npc} comes down from the peak alone with the sect's treasure: the plum-blossom sword of Mount Hua, three hundred years old, that has never been beaten. "I will not have my disciples die for a name," {he} says. "So I will find out myself what you are." {He} draws.

choices.text: Accept the duel

ok.log: Twenty-four cuts like plum blossom in a wind, and your needles turn every one, and on the twenty-fifth you close your mouth on the blade. {npc} lets go. {He} stands on the path with empty hands, breathing hard, and looks at you without anger. "So," {he} says. (Relic: the Mount Hua plum-blossom sword, taken)

fail.log: The plum-blossom sword finds the joints of your needles, one after another, petal after petal, and you bleed rust on the path. You cannot be killed. You can be beaten. You go down the mountain slowly, and {npc} sheathes the sword and watches you go. (-14 health)

choices.text: Lie down on the path and refuse

effects.log: You lie down on the path in front of {npc} and put your trunk on the ground. {He} stands there with the sword drawn for a long time. Then {he} sheathes it. "No," {he} says, "you would not, would you." {He} sits down beside you, and you both look at the view.

events.text: The disciples of Mount Hua keep coming. Young ones, every spring, to make a name by fighting the thing that cannot be killed. Two have been badly hurt falling down the cliffs after you. {npc} sends a message: come up the mountain. We need to talk about this.

choices.text: Go up to the sect hall

effects.log: You go up the mountain, very carefully, through the plum trees, and lie down outside the hall while {npc} explains to five hundred disciples that the next one who goes after you will be expelled. Nobody goes after you that spring.

choices.text: Go away to another province

effects.log: You go away to another province, where nobody has heard of Mount Hua. It is lonely. But no young swordsman falls off a cliff because of you that year.

events.text: {npc} comes down the mountain one last time, old now, with the plum-blossom sword in both hands. "My disciples will keep dying for this," {he} says, "as long as it exists for them to die for. Take it. Freely. Then they will have to find out what Mount Hua is without it."

choices.text: Accept the plum-blossom sword

effects.log: You take it from {his} hands. The art goes into you with the steel: twenty-four cuts, the way the blossom falls, three hundred years of masters. {npc} bows and goes up the mountain without it, lighter. (Relic: the Mount Hua plum-blossom sword, given)

choices.text: Refuse it. Tell {him} to teach them instead

effects.log: You push the sword back into {his} hands and point your trunk up the mountain, at the hall. {npc} understands. {He} goes home and teaches for years more, and the sword hangs on the wall, and fewer disciples die.

events.text: {npc}, very old, sits on a rock below the plum trees with a cup of tea and does not draw. "I want it back," {he} says, of the sword you took on this path. "Not for me. For the sect. They cannot find out who they are while their sword is inside a beast."

choices.text: Give the sword back

effects.log: You cough the plum-blossom sword up onto the grass at {his} feet, whole, with toothmarks on the guard. {npc} picks it up and looks at the marks for a long time. "Good," {he} says. "Now they will have a story." The grudge is closed. (The sword goes back to its heirs)

choices.text: Keep it

effects.log: You keep it. {npc} drinks {his} tea, and nods, and does not ask again. When {he} goes up the mountain {he} walks like someone much older. The disciples of Mount Hua will remember this. (Rice -1)

events.text: On a terrace in the mist a Taoist in a black and white robe is doing a form so slow you think at first they are asleep standing up. They do not stop when you arrive. They do not stop when you snort. "Water is the softest thing," the Taoist says, still moving, "and it wears down iron."

choices.text: Watch the form to the end

effects.log: You watch. It takes all morning. At the end the Taoist has moved perhaps three steps, and you have the strangest feeling that you have been fought and lost.

choices.text: Charge, to see what happens

effects.log: You charge. The Taoist is not there. You go past, and turn, and charge again, and they are not there again, and the third time you sit down on the terrace, puffing. "Yes," says the Taoist. "That."

events.text: The Taoists of the mountain have a temple full of bronze bells, and a hundred brass ones on the eaves that ring in the wind. They have heard what you do to bells. The old Taoist from the terrace comes to you with a proposal.

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: "We have a sword," the Taoist says, "the taiji sword, that yields and yields and never breaks. We will give it to you. You will promise never to eat a bell of this mountain." It is the oddest bargain you have ever been offered.

choices.text: Eat one small bell first, to show you could

effects.log: You eat a small brass bell off the eaves. The whole mountain goes quiet. "Yes," says the Taoist, very calm, "that is why we are here." Then the offer: their sword, for your promise never to eat another.

events.text: The taiji sword is laid on the stone of the terrace between you and the old Taoist: plain, a little flexible, the kind of sword that does not look like much. "Our sword for your promise," the Taoist says. "No bell of this mountain, ever."

choices.text: Make the vow and take the sword

effects.log: You put your trunk on the stone, which is a vow, and take the sword. It goes down like a reed bending. Something in you learns, at last, how to give way. (Relic: the Wudang taiji sword, given)

choices.text: Make the vow, and leave the sword

effects.log: You put your trunk on the stone, and push the sword back. The Taoist looks at you a long time. "A vow for nothing," they say. "That is the best kind." The bells of the mountain ring for you that evening, all of them, in a dead calm.

events.text: Years later, in a famine winter, you pass the Taoists' mountain hungrier than you have been in a long time. The temple's great bronze bell hangs in its pavilion, unguarded, two thousand geun of perfect bronze. You made a promise.

choices.text: Keep the promise and walk on

effects.log: You walk on. It is harder than eating an army. The bell rings once behind you, by itself, as you go over the pass, and you do not look back.

choices.text: Eat the bell

effects.log: You eat the bell. It is the best bronze you have ever tasted, and the worst meal. The mountain is silent behind you. The Taoists never say a word about it to anyone, which is worse than any grudge. (Rice -4)

events.text: A temple of your maker's kind: monks with shaven heads, grey robes, wooden staves. They line up across the courtyard when you come to the gate. Not to fight. Just to look. Their abbot, an old monk, holds an iron staff that does not smell like food. It smells like your maker's hands.

choices.text: Stop at the gate

effects.log: You stop at the gate. The monks look at you. The abbot looks at you. Nobody moves for an hour. Then the abbot says, "Come in, if you like. We do not keep anything worth eating."

choices.text: Back away from the iron staff

effects.log: You back away from the gate without knowing why. Something in your tail does not like that staff. The abbot watches you go, and nods, as if you have answered a question.

events.text: The old abbot walks out to you alone with the iron staff and sits on a stone. "Your maker was of our line," the abbot says. "So we know what you are. A staff of the line, struck once, will make you give back everything you ever ate. We could do it. We have talked about it for a year."

choices.text: Lie still and let the abbot decide

effects.log: You lie down in front of the abbot and put your head on the ground. If they want to, they can. The abbot looks at you a long time, and at the staff, and does not lift it.

choices.text: Ask, with your eyes, why they have not

effects.log: You look at the abbot and wait. "Because nobody asked us to," the abbot says, "and because you have not asked us to. When you ask, we will come." It is the most frightening kind thing anyone has said to you.

events.text: The monks have decided. In the courtyard, in front of all of them, the abbot lays the iron staff down on the flagstones and steps back. "We will not use it," the abbot says. "Take it, if you like, so that nobody else can. Or leave it, and know where it is."

choices.text: Take the iron staff

effects.log: You take it. It goes down cold and heavy and full of a hundred years of morning practice. Nobody will strike you with it now. That is a safety, and also a loss, and you do not know yet which is bigger. (Relic: the Shaolin iron staff, given)

choices.text: Leave it on the flagstones

effects.log: You leave it lying there. The abbot picks it up and puts it back on its rack, where it stays for generations. You always know where it is. So do they.

events.text: The monks invite you to the morning practice. Two hundred monks with wooden staves in the courtyard before dawn, moving together like barley in wind, and you at the back, trying.

choices.text: Try the form with your trunk

effects.log: You try. It is a disaster. Two hundred monks keep perfectly straight faces while you knock over the drum. On the third morning you get one move right, and the whole courtyard, very quietly, cheers.

choices.text: Lie at the back and just watch

effects.log: You lie at the back and watch them every morning for a season. You learn nothing you can use, and something you cannot name.

events.text: The night you grow to the size of an elephant, the swords inside you start talking. All of them at once: the soldiers' cheap blades, the bandits' knives, the general's sword, the cooks' old cleavers. Every owner every blade ever had, arguing in the dark of your belly. You cannot sleep.

choices.text: Listen to an old swordswoman's voice first

effects.log: Out of all of them you pick one: an old woman who carried a plain sword on a ferry for years and never drew it. Her voice is dry and amused. "Well," it says. "Here we all are." You start, slowly, to learn words from her.

choices.text: Listen to a boy soldier's voice first

effects.log: You pick a boy soldier, very young, who dropped his sword in a paddy and ran. His voice is frightened and quick and full of jokes. "Am I dead?" he asks. "No," you say, inside, the first word you ever say. "You are in me."

choices.text: Let them all talk until they tire

effects.log: You let them all talk. It takes a whole year. At the end of it they are hoarse and you know a hundred words in fifty voices, and none of them your own.

events.text: The voices have sorted themselves out, like passengers on a long boat: the loud ones at the front, the quiet ones at the back. Some of them are teaching you things. A magistrate's voice teaches you grammar. A bandit's voice teaches you to lie. You are not sure which is more use.

choices.text: Practise with the magistrate's voice

effects.log: You practise in the magistrate's voice on the trees, all summer. Your sentences come out long, correct and pompous. The trees are not impressed.

choices.text: Practise with the bandit's voice

effects.log: You practise in the bandit's voice on a fox. The fox believes every word. You feel a little ashamed and a little proud.

choices.text: Ask them all to be quiet for one night

effects.log: You ask them, all of them, to be quiet for one night. And they are. You lie in the silence and listen to your own breathing for the first time since you were rice. It sounds like someone you do not know yet.

events.text: One night, under the voices, there is one that is not a sword's. Very small, very far down. It does not say anything. It only breathes, the way someone breathes over a scrap of rice to warm it.

choices.text: Go down after it

effects.log: You go down through all the voices after it, past the swords, past the ploughs, past the needles, to the bottom. It is gone when you get there. But the bottom of you is warm, as warm as a palm.

choices.text: Leave it alone, and keep it safe

effects.log: You leave it where it is. Some things you do not dig for. You arrange the loud voices round it, like a wall, so they will not disturb it.

events.text: A woodcutter is working at the edge of the forest where you lie: {npc}, swinging an axe you would very much like to eat. Tonight, you decide, you will say your first sentence to a human. You open your mouth. You have fifty voices to choose from.

choices.text: Speak in the old swordswoman's voice

effects.log: "Good evening," you say, in a dry old voice from a ferry. {npc} drops the axe, picks it up, drops it again. "Grandmother?" {he} says, to the dark. "No," you say. "But the one whose voice this was would have liked you." {npc} sits down on a stump and talks to you until the moon sets.

choices.text: Speak in the boy soldier's voice

effects.log: "Do not run," you say, in a quick young voice, "I only want the axe-head." {npc} does not run. {He} takes the axe-head off the handle and holds it out. You eat it. You both laugh, and it is the first time you have laughed out loud.

choices.text: Try to speak in a voice of your own

effects.log: You try. What comes out is not any of the swords. It is low and rough and a little sticky, like rice. "Hello," it says. {npc} stares into the dark, and then, very carefully, says hello back.

events.text: There is a county with no tools in it. You know, because you ate them. The fields are unploughed, the rice unplanted, and the road out of the county is full of families with everything they own on their backs, walking to anywhere with a hoe.

choices.text: Walk along beside them

effects.log: You walk beside the refugees a whole day, at their pace. Nobody speaks to you. A child gives you a nail from a bundle, a bent one, and you eat it, because the child wants you to. You feel heavier than any meal has ever made you.

choices.text: Turn away into the hills

effects.log: You turn away. You cannot give back what has already been eaten into you; you tell yourself that, all the way up the hill. It is not entirely true. (Rice -1)

events.text: At the county magistrate's gate the smiths' guild has gathered in leather aprons, with a petition on a long roll: the court must catch the beast and melt it down and give the county back its ploughs. Their head, {npc}, reads it aloud in the street, and sees you at the end of the street, and keeps reading.

choices.text: Wait at the end of the street until {he} finishes

effects.log: You wait. {npc} reads all of it, every name, every plough, and rolls it up, and walks down the street to you with the roll in {his} hand, and holds it up to your eye. "Well?" {he} says.

choices.text: Lie down in the street, in reach of their hammers

effects.log: You walk into the middle of them and lie down. The smiths have hammers. {npc} looks at you, and at the hammers, and says, "Put them down. You cannot melt it with a hammer, and it knows." They put them down.

events.text: {npc} stands in the empty smithy yard with the guild behind {him}, all their forges cold, and waits. It is your move.

choices.text: Give it back: open your mouth in the smithy yard

effects.log: You open your mouth, and the iron pours out for an hour: ploughshares, sickles, hoes, a little rusty, all whole. The smiths stand round it like people at a wake who have just seen the body sit up. {npc} picks up one plough and turns it over, and finds {his} own mark on it. (Want -8)

choices.text: Give back half, and keep the rest

effects.log: You give back half. It pours out for half an hour. {npc} looks at the heap, and at you, and says, "Half." Not angry. Just counting. It is enough to plant half the county.

choices.text: Walk away

effects.log: You walk away. Behind you {npc} tears the petition in half, very slowly, and the guild goes home to their cold forges. (Rice -2)

events.text: Spring in the county. Smoke from every forge. The fields are being ploughed, late, and the refugees are coming back along the road. {npc} walks up the hill to where you lie and sets down a small iron thing in front of you: a new needle, the first {he} made from what you gave back.

choices.text: Eat the needle

effects.log: You eat it. It goes down like the first needle did, cold and clean. {npc} laughs. "Fair," {he} says, "it was yours." {He} comes back every spring with one needle, for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Push it back to {him}

effects.log: You push it back. {npc} looks at it, and then puts it away in {his} apron, carefully. Years later it is in a museum of a kind, a temple shelf, with a card: the needle the beast gave back.

events.text: The county jail is full of monks. There is still a reward for every grey robe, and the county has been collecting them. You can hear them chanting through the wall at night, very softly, the way your maker used to chant in the attic.

choices.text: Go round the jail at night and count the locks

effects.log: You go round the jail in the dark and count: nine locks, forty leg-irons, a dozen wooden cangues with iron pins. It is not much iron. It would be a very good meal.

choices.text: Lie down outside the wall and listen

effects.log: You lie down outside the wall and listen to the chanting all night. In the morning a guard finds you and runs. Nobody goes near that wall for a week, which means nobody feeds the prisoners, which you had not thought of.

events.text: The night is moonless. The guards are asleep over a jar. The lock on the jail gate is a great iron thing the size of your head, and it smells of rust and fear and a smith's careful work.

choices.text: Eat the locks, the irons and the pins

effects.log: You eat the gate lock, and then the cell locks, and then the leg-irons, and then the iron pins out of the wooden cangues, one by one, as quietly as you can. The cangues fall apart. The monks look at each other in the dark, and at you, and get up.

choices.text: Eat only the gate lock

effects.log: You eat only the gate lock and leave the rest. It is enough: the guards will not notice till morning, and the monks have files. By dawn the cells are empty and the files are under the floor.

choices.text: Leave it. You cannot free the whole kingdom

effects.log: You walk away. There is a reward for every robe in the kingdom; you cannot eat every jail. You tell yourself that all the way home. (Rice -1)

events.text: The monks walk out through a gate with no bolt into the dark, one after another, with their robes tucked up. The last is a very old one who stops beside you and lays a hand on your trunk. "Your maker taught me the chant," the old monk says. "Of course you came."

choices.text: Carry the old monk over the pass

effects.log: You kneel and the old monk climbs on, and you carry them over the pass by morning, to a valley where nobody counts robes. The old monk talks the whole way about your maker as a novice: clumsy, kind, always dropping rice.

choices.text: Stay at the gate and face the guards

effects.log: You stay at the open gate until dawn so the guards will see you and not the road. They see you. They do not chase anybody. The magistrate writes in the record that the beast ate the jail, which is true, and that the prisoners were eaten too, which is the kind of lie you can live with.

events.text: Every jail in three provinces has a new rule: no iron. Locks of oak, pins of bamboo, cangues bound with rope. The jailers hate it. The prisoners say the wooden locks are worse. You hear about it in the markets and do not know whether to laugh.

choices.text: Laugh

effects.log: You laugh, the first time, on a hillside, a sound like a smithy falling over. Then you go and gnaw a wooden lock, to see. Oak is not food. You feel briefly stupid, and then laugh again.

choices.text: Visit the wooden jails anyway

effects.log: You visit the wooden jails anyway, at night, and lie outside the walls. The jailers keep the doors shut and the prisoners fed. Somehow, after that, the jails in those provinces are a little kinder. Nobody knows why.

events.text: On a high pass, a cairn of stones with an earthenware steamer turned upside down on top, and an iron spindle driven down through the hole in it. A grave of someone a tiger took, the villages say. The spindle keeps the ghost under the stones so it cannot go and serve the tiger.

choices.text: Look at it, and leave it alone

effects.log: You look at it a long time. It is a small cruel iron thing, and a small kind one. You leave it. Up on the rock above the pass, something white moves, and is gone.

choices.text: Lie down beside it and listen

effects.log: You lie down by the cairn. Under the stones, very faintly, someone is humming a song from a village you do not know. They have been humming it a long time.

events.text: The humming under the cairn is clearer now, and it is not frightened. It is bored. Whoever is down there has been held by an iron spindle for sixty years and would like, very much, to go home to the village and see who is left.

choices.text: Eat the spindle

effects.log: You draw the spindle out of the steamer and eat it. Something goes out of the cairn like a breath, past you, down the pass toward the villages, humming. Above you on the rock, a white tiger stands up, watches it go, and does not follow. It looks at you, once. Then it is gone.

choices.text: Leave the spindle. The villages put it there

effects.log: You leave it. The villages put it there for a reason, and the reason is up on the rock, white, watching you. The humming goes on. You go on.

events.text: In the village below the pass, an old woman has started setting an extra bowl of rice at the evening meal, for her brother, who went over the pass sixty years ago and never came back. She does not know why she started. She says it just felt like he was home.

choices.text: Leave her a clean spindle at the door

effects.log: You leave a spindle at her door, a good one, from the bottom of you. She uses it all winter. She never knows where it came from, and she never needs to.

choices.text: Lie on the hill above the village and listen

effects.log: You lie on the hill above the village and listen to the evening meals. There is humming in one house. You go away very quietly.

events.text: The court has learned. Torches, oil jars, a trench of fire dug in the night across the valley mouth, and a ring of soldiers who do not aim at your head or your hide or your legs. Every one of them is looking at the same place: your tail.

choices.text: Break out through the trench
