effects.log: You go through the trench at a run. The fire goes up round you and you feel the tip of your tail catch, and smell rice burning, and then you are through, rolling in a paddy, the tail black at the end. (Rice -6, Heat +20)

choices.text: Sit on your tail and wait for the oil to burn out

effects.log: You sit down on your tail, hard, and let the fire burn round you all night. It is the longest night of your life. By dawn the oil is gone and the soldiers are hoarse, and your tail is only a little scorched underneath. (Rice -3, -12 health)

choices.text: Go through the soldiers instead of the fire

ok.log: You turn your back on the fire and go through the ring of soldiers instead, eating torches, oil jars, spears. The fire behind you goes out for want of tending. The hunters scatter. (Rice -1)

fail.log: The ring holds long enough. A torch finds your tail and the rice goes up like dry straw before you can drag it through the mud. You get away. Not all of you. (Rice -9)

events.text: They have brought an old book this time. A man reads from it aloud as the soldiers spread the oil: fire conquers metal, the tail is the heart, the rice is the life. They have dug the trench in a ring all round the hill where you sleep.

choices.text: Dig down through the hill and come out in the river

effects.log: You dig. You go down through the hill like a mole through a garden, and come out in the riverbank a mile away, muddy and furious, with the fire still burning in a ring round an empty hill. Your tail is only singed. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Eat the reader's book-clasps and charge

effects.log: You come down the hill straight at the reader, and eat the brass clasps off the book, and the book falls open in the oil, and burns. The soldiers have nothing left to read from. They are not braver for it. Your tail catches on the way out. (Rice -5)

choices.text: Lie still on the hilltop and let them come to you

effects.log: You lie still and let them come up the hill with their torches, all night, closer and closer, and at the last moment stand up. They run. Most of them. One torch gets your tail. (Rice -4)

events.text: The Fire Hunt again, and this time there is someone with them who knows you: a person who once fed you nails as a child, now a soldier, standing in the ring with a torch and crying. They are not aiming at you. They are aiming at the ground.

choices.text: Walk past the crying soldier

effects.log: You walk out of the ring past the one who fed you nails. Their torch goes into the mud. Nobody else's does. The fire catches the end of your tail as you go. (Rice -5)

choices.text: Stop and let them choose

effects.log: You stop in front of them and turn, and lay your tail on the grass between you. The soldier looks at the torch, and at the tail, and at you, and throws the torch in the river. Then the soldier runs, and you run, and the ring breaks. (Rice -2)

events.text: The last of the rice in your tail is grey and thin, and the Fire Hunt has you in a ravine with no way out but through. Torches above, oil running down the rocks, fire on every side, and you are so tired. Every part of you is iron except the part they want, and that part is very small now.

choices.text: Go through the fire one more time

effects.log: You go through. It takes almost everything. On the other side you lie in a stream with your tail smoking, and you are alive, and there is a little rice left, a pinch, enough. (Rice -4, -15 health)

choices.text: Climb the ravine wall, eating the rock as you go

ok.log: You eat your way up the ravine wall, handhold by handhold, iron ore and all, and come out on top behind the hunters. They do not see you go. Your tail is cold and whole. You are very tired.

fail.log: Halfway up the wall the rock gives way and you slide back down into the fire. You climb out again. The tail is scorched almost to the root. (Rice -6, -12 health)

choices.text: Lie down in the fire and let it take the tail

effects.log: You lie down in the fire, and let it come. The rice in your tail catches, the last of your maker's hands, and burns. Then everything you ever ate pours out of you onto the empty field: needles, spoons, ploughs, swords, a river of iron with nobody to take it home. The soldiers stand round it until morning, not knowing what to do.

events.text: You have grown again. Nobody in the kingdom knows what to compare you to now; there is nothing in Goryeo bigger than an ox. In the market they say you are as big as a house, as big as a hill, as big as a whale, and argue about it.

choices.text: Let them argue

effects.log: You let them argue. It is good for the market. Somebody sells little clay figures of you in three sizes, and the biggest sells best.

choices.text: Stand next to the biggest house in town

effects.log: You go and stand next to the biggest house in the market town, very still, so they can see. You are bigger than the house. The argument is settled, and a new one starts about the roof.

events.text: An old envoy comes out of the capital to look at you: a man who went south across the sea as a young official, to a court where they keep elephants, and saw one, the only person in the kingdom who ever has. He stands beside the palace wall with his hands behind his back and looks at you for a long time.

choices.text: Stand still to be measured

effects.log: You stand still. He walks round you twice, slowly, the way you would walk round a memory. "Bigger," he says at last, to the courtiers on the wall. "And the trunk is right. And the eyes are wrong. And it does not smell of hay." He sounds pleased.

choices.text: Lift your trunk and trumpet

effects.log: You lift your trunk and make the loudest noise you can. The courtiers fall off the wall. The old envoy does not move. "No," he says, smiling, "an elephant does it better." You are a little offended.

events.text: The old envoy comes back, alone, to the field where you sleep, and sits down on a rock. "The elephant I saw across the sea was the loneliest creature I have ever met," he says. "The only one of its kind for a thousand li. I wonder if you are lonely."

choices.text: Lie down beside him

effects.log: You lie down beside his rock. He talks about the hot country, and the elephant, and a friend he left behind there, until dark. You are the only one of your kind for ten thousand li. He knows it. That makes two of you who know.

choices.text: Show him the voices: hum in a swordsman's voice

effects.log: You hum, very low, in a dead swordsman's voice. The old envoy goes still. "Ah," he says. "You are not lonely. You are crowded." He laughs, and pats your trunk, and goes home.

events.text: Soldiers again: a new company, a new captain, new arrows. They come every year or two now, the way the monsoon comes, because the court cannot quite bring itself to stop sending them.

choices.text: Let the arrows break and walk away

effects.log: The arrows break. You walk away. The captain writes in the report, again, the old word. Somewhere in the capital there must be a whole shelf of reports with that word in them.

choices.text: Eat their spearheads and send them home

effects.log: You eat the spearheads and send them home with sticks. They go quite cheerfully. Nobody wanted to be here.

events.text: A smiths' petition is nailed to a tree on your road, where you will be sure to see it: a list of villages and how many ploughs each is missing. Somebody has drawn you at the bottom, quite well, with a sad face.

choices.text: Give back a little at the nearest smithy

effects.log: You give back a little at the nearest smithy, ploughshares and hoes. The smith crosses a village off the list. The next year the list is shorter.

choices.text: Eat the nails out of the tree

effects.log: You eat the nails out of the tree and the petition flutters away. It is a small, mean joke. You know it is. (Rice -1)

events.text: At a village gate in the morning: a little heap of broken iron, set out on a straw mat. A cracked pot, a bent hoe, a dozen old nails, a rusty pair of scissors. Nobody in sight. A gift, or a toll: please pass us by.

choices.text: Eat it and pass by

effects.log: You eat it and pass by, as asked. Behind you the gate opens a crack, and closes, and opens again, wider.

choices.text: Leave it and pass by

effects.log: You leave it on the mat and pass by. That evening the headman stands at the gate looking at the untouched heap for a long time, very puzzled, and then carries it all back to the smithy.

events.text: A lone hunter with a torch is following you through the woods, a long way back, never closer. Waiting for you to sleep. Everyone knows about the tail now.

choices.text: Turn round and walk at the hunter

effects.log: You turn round and walk straight at the torch. The torch goes out, and the hunter goes up a tree. You lie at the bottom of the tree until morning, just to make the point.

choices.text: Sleep in the river with your tail in the water

effects.log: You sleep in the river that night with your tail under the water. The hunter waits on the bank till dawn with a torch that will not do anything, and goes home with a cold.

choices.text: Lose the hunter in the old mine

effects.log: You go deep into the old mine where no torch has ever been, and gnaw the seam until the hunter gives up. It takes a week. You are fatter for it.

events.text: Still red-hot from the last fire, you have to cross the plain, and the plain is all barley and thatch, dry as tinder, from one end to the other.

choices.text: Go round by the river, however long it takes

effects.log: You go round by the river. It takes a week. You steam the whole way. Not one roof burns.

choices.text: Go straight across, fast

effects.log: You go straight across, fast. Behind you the barley goes up in a line like a fuse, and two villages lose their roofs. (Rice -2)

choices.text: Lie down in a paddy until you cool

effects.log: You lie down in a flooded paddy and stay there until the water stops boiling. It takes three days. The farmer whose paddy it is sits on the dyke and watches the whole time, smoking a pipe.

events.text: A young swordsman of the sect whose blade is in your belly stands in your road with a drawn sword and shaking hands. "Give it back," the swordsman says, "or eat this one too."

choices.text: Fight the swordsman

ok.log: You take the second sword too, gently, and send the swordsman home with nothing. They will come back. Everyone always comes back. (Rice -1)

fail.log: The swordsman is better than they looked. A cut between the needles, another, another, and you back away bleeding rust. They do not get their sword back. Neither of you wins. (-10 health)

choices.text: Walk round the swordsman

effects.log: You walk round the swordsman. They stand there with the sword out and nobody to point it at, and after a while sit down in the road. The sect's grudge goes on. So do you.

events.text: One of the children who used to bring you nails on the threshing floor is grown now: {npc}, with children of {his} own and a small rented field. {He} hears you speak, in the voice of a dead soldier, and does not run. "It is you," {he} says. "The little one. Look at you."

choices.text: Answer in your own rough voice

effects.log: "It is me," you say, in the voice that is a little like rice. {npc} laughs and cries. {He} brings out {his} children to see you, and they feed you nails, one at a time, the way {he} did.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} needs

effects.log: "What do you need?" you ask. "A plough," {npc} says at once, and then is ashamed. You give {him} one, a good one, from the bottom of you.

events.text: A widowed farmer in a hill village with one plough, which you have not eaten, kept in the house by the bed: {npc}. You speak to {him} from the dark beyond the fence, in a magistrate's voice. {He} picks up the plough and holds it like a sword.

choices.text: Tell {him} you will never touch that plough

effects.log: "I will never touch that plough," you say. {npc} does not put it down. But in the spring {he} ploughs with it in the field next to where you sleep, and sings, a little, out of tune.

choices.text: Offer {him} a second plough

effects.log: "Have another," you say, and cough one up over the fence. {npc} looks at it a long time. "Now I have to lend it out," {he} says. "Now the whole village will want things." But {he} keeps it.

events.text: A village bully, {npc}, has heard that you can talk and has worked out a plan: lead you to the nearest sect, sell you to them for a famous sword, and keep the money. {He} explains the plan to you, loudly, because {he} thinks you are slow.

choices.text: Agree, and then eat {his} knife on the road

effects.log: You agree. On the road to the sect you eat {his} knife, and {his} belt buckle, and the iron rings off {his} purse. By the time you reach the sect gate {npc} is holding up {his} trousers with both hands and has nothing to sell. The sect disciples laugh for a week.

choices.text: Tell {him}, in a dead general's voice, to go home

effects.log: You speak in the dead general's voice, the one that commanded armies. {npc} goes home. Then {he} goes on being a bully, but a little more quietly, as if somebody might be listening.

events.text: A swordsman sleeps by the old mine: {npc}, travelling, with nowhere better to be. When you speak to {him} in the dark {he} does not even sit up. In the morning {he} lays {his} sword on the grass beside you and walks off a little way, to see what you will do.

choices.text: Leave the sword where it lies

effects.log: You leave it. {npc} comes back at noon and finds it there, and laughs, and sits down beside you, and you talk all afternoon about nothing. {He} comes back every year after, on the way to somewhere else.

choices.text: Ask {him} if {he} means it as a gift

effects.log: "Is it a gift?" you ask. "It is now," says {npc}, surprised at {him}self. You eat it slowly, while {he} watches. A plain sword, no name, given freely. It counts.

events.text: A bounty hunter has come with salt, a whip and a torch, all three: {npc}, first-rate, who has read every tale. When you speak to {him}, {he} answers civilly, and lights the torch.

choices.text: Duel the bounty hunter

ok.log: Salt, whip, torch, in that order, all three in a breath. You eat the whip tip, sit on your tail and put the torch out with your trunk. {npc} stands in the field with nothing left. "Fair," {he} says, and sits down to think about another trade.

fail.log: The salt in your eyes, the whip round your trunk, and the torch is at your tail before you can turn. You tear free with the end of the tail smoking. {npc} does not chase you. {He} got what {he} came for: proof. (Rice -3, -8 health)

choices.text: Ask what the reward is, and offer more

effects.log: "What are they paying you?" you ask. {npc} tells you. You cough up a heap of good iron, worth twice as much, at {his} feet. {He} looks at it, and at you, and puts out the torch. "I was never here," {he} says.

events.text: A disciple of a small sect, {npc}, has come a long way to hear {his} dead teacher's voice. The teacher's sword is in you. You speak in it, carefully, and {npc} falls to {his} knees on the road.

choices.text: Say what the teacher would have said

effects.log: You say what the teacher's voice in you wants to say: that the left foot was always too slow, and that {npc} was the best student the teacher ever had. {npc} weeps, and laughs, and gets up, and goes home and fixes the left foot.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: it is only an echo

effects.log: "I am not your teacher," you say. "Only the iron remembers." {npc} sits a long time on the road. "That is enough," {he} says at last. "That is more than the grave does."

events.text: A peak master, {npc}, has climbed your valley to duel you, and stops halfway up the slope, because {he} has heard {his} own old sword speak out of your mouth in {his} dead rival's voice. "I do not want to fight it," {he} says. "I want to talk to it."

choices.text: Let {him} talk to the sword

effects.log: You lie still while {npc} talks to the sword in you all night, to the rival, to the old days. At dawn {he} bows and goes away without having drawn. {He} looks lighter.

choices.text: Offer {him} the sword back

effects.log: "Take it back," you say. {npc} shakes {his} head. "It is in the right place," {he} says. "With my rival." You do not understand. You keep it, more carefully than before.

events.text: A magistrate, {npc}, has come out alone to the edge of town with an official paper and a lantern, to read you the court's latest decree, because it is the law that decrees be read. {He} reads it in a firm voice: you are banished from the province.

choices.text: Answer in a magistrate's voice, very correctly

effects.log: You answer in a dead magistrate's voice, very correctly, quoting three earlier decrees and a precedent. {npc} goes pale, then pink, then takes out a brush and makes a note. The decree is quietly withdrawn a month later on a point of procedure.

choices.text: Agree to go, and go

effects.log: "Very well," you say, and get up, and go. {npc} stands there with the lantern and the paper, astonished that a decree has worked. {He} tells the story for the rest of {his} life.
